t: Minimum Increment Operations to Make Array Beautiful
o: An array is beautiful when every window of length ≥ 3 contains an element ≥ k. Equivalently, no three consecutive elements are all below k — so chosen 'k-or-more' positions must have gaps of at most 3. Raising nums[i] to k costs max(0, k − nums[i]). Example 1 raises index 1 (cost 1) and index 4 (cost 2) for a total of 3.
k: Beautiful ⇔ there exist positions with nums[p] ≥ k such that consecutive chosen positions differ by ≤ 3 (covering all windows of size 3).
DP where dp[i] = min cost given position i is (one of) the chosen raised element(s): dp[i] = max(0,k−nums[i]) + min(dp[i−1], dp[i−2], dp[i−3]).

a.n: Approach 1: Linear DP with Window of Three
a.i: Treat it as a covering problem: pick a set of positions to raise to k such that gaps between picked positions (and from the start/end) never exceed 3. dp[i] is the cheapest way assuming i is picked; it extends the best of the three previous picks. The answer is the best dp among the last three indices, with virtual picks before the array costing 0.
s: Define dp[i] = cost(i) + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2], dp[i-3]) with out-of-range terms 0 and cost(i) = max(0, k − nums[i]).
a.sp: O(n) — DP array (reducible to O(1) with three rolling variables)

a.i: Since dp[i] looks back only three steps, keep just three previous values. Same recurrence, O(1) memory — worth mentioning as the production-quality refinement.
s: Keep p1, p2, p3 as dp[i-1], dp[i-2], dp[i-3].
Compute cur = min(p1,p2,p3) + cost, then shift variables.
After the loop return min of the last three stored values.

w: Lead with the reformulation 'no three consecutive elements below k' — it makes the DP obvious. Pitfall: use 64-bit sums (k and nums up to 10^9, n up to 10^5). Edge case: elements already ≥ k cost 0 and act as free anchors. Follow-up: generalize the window size to w.
